claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has severe lattice distortion arising from the random distribution of its constituent elements.
Lattice distortion in WTaTiVZr perturbs dislocation-core structures.
The perturbed dislocation cores produce wavy edge-dislocation lines in WTaTiVZr.
Wavy edge-dislocation configurations enhance dislocation mobility at high temperature.
The altered dislocation configuration enhances work hardening at high temperature.
Enhanced dislocation mobility and work hardening increase the plastic strain and toughness of WTaTiVZr relative to pure tungsten.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr initially forms a homogeneous, single-phase BCC state.
Compositional fluctuations distort the lattice of single-phase WTaTiVZr.
Temperatures of approximately 800–1000°C are representative of high-temperature plasma-facing-component service.
Using identical strain rates and atmospheres for WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten isolates intrinsic deformation-mechanism differences.
WTaTiVZr switches from the sluggish screw-dislocation motion typical of pure tungsten to more mobile, wavy edge-dislocation motion.
Increased work hardening and strain delocalization delay crack initiation and propagation in WTaTiVZr.
Under identical high-temperature tests, WTaTiVZr will have greater strain to failure than pure tungsten.
Under identical high-temperature tests, WTaTiVZr will absorb more energy and exhibit greater toughness than pure tungsten.
WTaTiVZr will show predominantly wavy edge dislocations, whereas pure tungsten will show predominantly screw dislocations.
Commercial pure tungsten has limited plastic strain and toughness because its deformation is constrained by relatively immobile screw dislocations.
The proposed mechanism is limited to high-temperature inert conditions without phase transformation, oxidation, or extensive radiation damage.
Processing-dependent changes in microstructural homogeneity may alter the proposed effect.
The magnitude of any improvement in plastic strain and toughness is not yet quantified.
